name: ATTINY87-XUR
title: ATtiny87/167 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 8K/16K bytes Flash and a LIN controller
summary: An 8-bit AVR RISC microcontroller family running from 1.8 V to 5.5 V at up to 16 MHz, with 8 Kbytes (ATtiny87) or 16 Kbytes (ATtiny167) of in-system programmable Flash, 512 bytes each of EEPROM and SRAM, and 16 I/O lines. Its peripherals include a LIN 2.1/1.3 controller that doubles as an 8-bit UART, an 8-bit asynchronous timer, a 16-bit timer whose two compare channels can each be steered to four pins, SPI, a USI, an 11-channel 10-bit ADC with differential gain stages, an analog comparator, a 100 µA current source for LIN node identification and a temperature sensor. Clock sources can be switched at run time. ATTINY87-XUR is the 8 Kbyte part in a 20-pin TSSOP.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator connections
circuits.description: A quartz crystal or ceramic resonator between XTAL2 (PB5) and XTAL1 (PB4), each pin loaded to ground by a capacitor. C1 and C2 are always equal; 12 pF to 22 pF is the starting range for crystals from 0.9 MHz to 16 MHz, and a ceramic resonator takes the values its own maker gives. The best value depends on the crystal, the stray capacitance and the noise around the board.
notes: The 0.4 - 0.9 MHz range is for ceramic resonators only.

circuits.title: Low-frequency crystal oscillator connections
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz watch crystal between XTAL2 (PB5) and XTAL1 (PB4), each pin with a 12 pF to 22 pF capacitor to ground. The capacitors may be needed when the parasitic load of the pads, wiring and board is very low. The same crystal can clock Timer/Counter0 asynchronously while neither the high-frequency crystal oscillator nor the external clock is in use.

circuits.title: External clock drive configuration
circuits.description: An outside clock signal drives CLKI (XTAL1, PB4) and shares the part's ground; CKSEL or CSEL must select the external clock (0000). XTAL2 (PB5) is not used by the clock and stays free as I/O or CLKO.

circuits.title: Current source with an external resistor
circuits.description: The 100 µA source drives the ISRC pin (PA3, shared with ADC3) into a resistor to ground, and the ADC reads the resulting voltage. Used for LIN node addressing, where the resistor value is the node's address (1 kΩ to 27 kΩ for 8 or 16 addresses at AVCC = 5 V), for reading a resistive sensor, or as a voltage or comparator threshold reference.

parts.note: 0.5% suggested; 30 kΩ largest at AVCC = 5 V, 15 kΩ at 3 V

notes: ISRCEN switches the source on; the source runs from AVCC.

circuits.title: debugWIRE setup
circuits.description: The debugger reaches the part over one line on the RESET pin (PB7, dW) with a common ground; VCC is 1.8 V to 5.5 V. Any pull-up on the line must be 10 kΩ or more, and no capacitor or other reset source may be on it.

circuits.title: Parallel programming
circuits.description: High-voltage parallel programming: VCC and AVCC at 4.5 V to 5.5 V, +12 V on RESET (PB7), the control inputs WR, XA0, XA1/BS2, PAGEL/BS1 and OE on PB0, PB1, PB2, PB3 and PB5, a pulsed clock on XTAL1 (PB4), the RDY/BSY status output on PB6 and the bidirectional 8-bit data bus on PA7 to PA0.
notes: AVCC stays within VCC ± 0.3 V and always within 4.5 V to 5.5 V.

circuits.title: Serial programming and verify
circuits.description: In-system programming over SPI: MOSI into PA4, MISO out of PA2, SCK into PA5, RESET (PB7) driven by the programmer, VCC 1.8 V to 5.5 V. With the internal oscillator selected no clock is needed on XTAL1.

operation.text: The two parts run the same code on the same hardware; only the Flash size differs (8 Kbytes against 16 Kbytes). Both have 512 bytes of EEPROM and 512 bytes of SRAM.
Projected from qualification: data retention failures well below 1 PPM after 20 years at 85 °C, or after 100 years at 25 °C.
Typical figures come from simulation and from characterising other AVR parts on the same process; minimum and maximum values follow once the part itself is characterised.

A Harvard machine with separate program and data buses and a one-stage pipeline: the next instruction is fetched while the current one runs, so most instructions take one clock. The 32 x 8-bit register file feeds two operands to the ALU and takes the result back within a single cycle. Most instructions are one 16-bit word; each program address holds a 16- or 32-bit instruction.
SREG is updated after every ALU operation. It is not saved or restored automatically on interrupt entry or return; software must do it.

R26 to R31 pair up as the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers for indirect data addressing, with displacement, post-increment and pre-decrement. Z can also point into Flash for table lookups. The 32 registers also sit at data addresses 0x00 to 0x1F.

The stack lives in SRAM and grows downward; the stack pointer must be set above 0x60 before any call or interrupt. PUSH lowers it by one, a call or interrupt by two; POP raises it by one, RET and RETI by two. It is held in SPH and SPL in I/O space and resets to the end of internal SRAM.

Each interrupt has its own vector and enable bit and also needs the global I bit in SREG. A lower vector address means higher priority; RESET is highest, then INT0. Entering an interrupt clears I; RETI sets it again. Flag-type interrupts are remembered while disabled and served in priority order once enabled; level-type interrupts fire only while the condition lasts. After returning from an interrupt one main-program instruction runs before any pending interrupt. CLI takes effect at once; the instruction after SEI runs before any pending interrupt.

At least four clock cycles pass before the vector runs, during which the PC is pushed; the jump at the vector takes three more. A multi-cycle instruction in progress finishes first. Waking from sleep adds four cycles on top of the start-up time. A return from interrupt takes four cycles.
16 bits wide, at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. There is no separate boot section: SPM can run from anywhere in Flash. Constant tables can be placed anywhere and read with LPM.

Data addresses run: the register file (32 bytes, 0x0000-0x001F), standard I/O (64 bytes, 0x0020-0x005F), extended I/O (160 bytes, 0x0060-0x00FF), then 512 bytes of internal SRAM (0x0100-0x02FF). Extended I/O is reached only with LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD. Addressing modes are direct, indirect, indirect with displacement (up to 63 locations from Y or Z), pre-decrement and post-increment. An SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

512 bytes in a separate space, byte read and write, at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. A read halts the CPU for four cycles, a write for two. A write starts only when EEPE is set within four cycles of setting EEMPE. EEPM bits choose atomic erase-and-write (00), erase only (01) or write only (10); a write-only to an unerased byte leaves its contents undefined. No other EEPROM access is possible while one is in progress. Write timing comes from the calibrated RC oscillator, so OSCCAL must keep it in range.

Too low a supply can spoil an EEPROM write or make the CPU run wrongly. Holding the part in reset while the supply is low, by the brown-out detector or an external supervisor, prevents it; a write already under way when reset arrives still completes if the supply holds.

Registers at I/O 0x00-0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI, CBI, SBIS and SBIC. IN and OUT reach 0x00-0x3F; as data addresses add 0x20. SBI and CBI touch only the named bit, so they are safe on registers holding write-one-to-clear flags. Reserved bits should be written zero and reserved addresses never written. Three general purpose I/O registers are provided for flags and variables.

clkCPU drives the core, registers and stack; clkI/O drives most peripherals and the synchronous external interrupt logic; clkFLASH runs the Flash interface alongside clkCPU; clkASY lets Timer/Counter0 run from an external clock or 32 kHz crystal, even in sleep; clkADC is separate so the CPU and I/O clocks can be stopped during a conversion.

External clock, the 8 MHz calibrated RC oscillator, the 128 kHz watchdog oscillator, a 32.768 kHz low-frequency crystal oscillator, or a crystal/ceramic resonator oscillator in four ranges from 0.4 MHz to 16 MHz. The CKSEL fuses pick the source at reset; afterwards software can switch to any other through CLKSELR. Waking from power-down or power-save, or enabling a new source, waits out the source's start-up count; a reset start adds a delay timed by the watchdog oscillator.

At reset the CKSEL and SUT fuses are copied into CLKSELR. Parts ship with CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10 and CKDIV8 programmed: the internal 8 MHz RC oscillator, longest start-up, divided by 8 (1 MHz). Programmers must allow for this slow default clock.

About 8.0 MHz with no external parts, varying with voltage and temperature. The factory calibration is loaded into OSCCAL at reset; software can tune OSCCAL further. CAL7 picks one of two overlapping ranges and CAL[6:0] tunes within it (0x7F gives a higher frequency than 0x80). Since this oscillator times EEPROM and Flash writes, it must not be set above 8.8 MHz while writing them. The watchdog oscillator still times the watchdog and reset time-out.
A low-power 128 kHz oscillator, nominal at 3 V and 25 °C, selectable as the system clock.

XTAL1 (PB4) and XTAL2 (PB5) are the input and output of an inverting amplifier for a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. CKSEL[3:1] picks the frequency range; CKSEL0 with SUT[1:0] picks the start-up time.
Runs a 32.768 kHz watch crystal as the system clock. The asynchronous timer can also start and use this oscillator when neither the high-frequency crystal oscillator nor the external clock is on.
A clock driven into CLKI (PB4). The asynchronous timer can use this input when neither crystal oscillator is running.

When no crystal oscillator is used, the system clock can be put out on CLKO (PB5) by programming the CKOUT fuse or the COUT bit in CLKSELR; it overrides the pin's I/O function, and with the prescaler in use the divided clock is the one output.

Clock sources can be turned on and off at run time, de-glitched, under software control through CLKCSR, which takes one command at a time after a timed enable write: disable source (0x01), enable source (0x02), request clock availability, switch source (0x04), recover system clock source (0x05) and enable watchdog in automatic reload mode (0x06). CLKSELR holds the CSEL, CSUT and COUT values the commands use. Enabling a source starts a cycle count set by CSUT; CLKRDY reads 1 once the source is ready. Disable is refused for the source now clocking the system. Several sources may run at once, but only one of the three external sources at a time, and the external clock and low-frequency oscillator enables are shared with the asynchronous timer.

Targets are the 8 MHz RC, the 128 kHz watchdog oscillator, the external clock, the low-frequency oscillator or the crystal/resonator. With interrupts off: enable the new source, wait for CLKRDY, issue the switch command, confirm it with the recover command, then disable the old source.

The watchdog can check that the system clock runs, either by normal software reloads or by automatic hardware reloading started with one command; the two are exclusive and meaningful only when the reset clock source is internal. In automatic reload mode only the watchdog reset works (no interrupt), WDP[3:0] still set the period, and only a reset ends the mode. Only clocks of at least four times the watchdog clock frequency can be monitored. The mode should be started before switching to an external source.

CLKPR divides clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH for any clock source, to save power when less speed is needed. Switching is glitch-free and never passes through a frequency above both the old and the new setting.

Four modes, chosen with SM[1:0] and entered by setting SE and executing SLEEP: Idle (00), ADC Noise Reduction (01), Power-down (10) and Power-save (11). A wake-up interrupt halts the MCU four cycles beyond the start-up time, runs the handler, then continues after SLEEP; register file and SRAM keep their contents. A reset during sleep restarts from the reset vector.

In power-down and power-save, setting BODS in MCUCR (by a timed sequence) turns the fuse-enabled brown-out detector off while asleep, saving its current; it turns back on at wake-up, which then takes about 60 µs.

Stops clkCPU and clkFLASH; SPI, analog comparator, ADC, USI start detector, asynchronous timer, watchdog and interrupts keep running. Turning off the comparator with ACD saves more. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

Also stops clkI/O; the ADC, external interrupts, USI start detector, asynchronous timer and watchdog keep running. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake-up comes from ADC complete, external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out, USI start, asynchronous timer, SPM/EEPROM ready, any pin change, or INT0/INT1 set for level triggering.

The external oscillator stops; only asynchronous logic runs. Wake-up comes from external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out, USI start condition, any pin change, or INT0/INT1 set for level triggering. A level used to wake must be held until start-up ends. The wake-up delay is the same reset time-out the CKSEL fuses set.

As power-down, except that Timer/Counter0 keeps running when clocked asynchronously (AS0 set) and can wake the part on overflow or compare match. Without asynchronous clocking power-down should be used, as the asynchronous timer's registers are undefined after waking from power-save with AS0 = 0.

PRR stops the clock to single peripherals in active and idle modes. The stopped peripheral keeps its state, its registers cannot be accessed, and it resumes as it was when its bit is cleared; it should normally be disabled first.

Turn off what is unused before sleeping: the ADC (an enabled ADC stays on in every sleep mode, and its next conversion after re-enabling is an extended one), the analog comparator (and in every mode if it uses the internal reference), the brown-out detector, the internal reference output, the current source and the watchdog, all of which otherwise draw current in deep sleep. Pins should drive no resistive loads; input buffers are off in modes where clkI/O and clkADC are stopped, except where needed for wake-up. A floating input or one near VCC/2 draws excess current, so analog inputs should have their digital buffers disabled in DIDR0 and DIDR1. An enabled debugWIRE (DWEN) keeps the main clock running in sleep.

All I/O registers take their initial values and execution starts at the reset vector, which must hold an RJMP to the reset handler. Ports go to their reset state at once, with no clock needed. After the last reset source releases, a delay counter set by SUT and CKSEL stretches the internal reset.

Power-on reset (supply below VPOT), external reset (low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse), watchdog system reset, and brown-out reset (supply below VBOT with the detector on). MCUSR flags which occurred: PORF, EXTRF, BORF, WDRF; read and clear it early in the program.
An on-chip detector holds the part in reset while VCC is below the detection level and starts the delay counter once it is passed; reset reasserts without delay when VCC falls back below it.

A low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part even with no clock; shorter pulses may not. The time-out starts when the pin rises through VRST. Programming RSTDISBL turns the pin into PB7 I/O, leaving power-on and brown-out as reset sources; while it is RESET, DDB7, PORTB7 and PINB7 read 0.
Compares VCC against a level set by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis. Falling below VBOT- resets the part at once; rising above VBOT+ starts the time-out. A dip shorter than tBOD is not detected.
A watchdog time-out gives a one-CK reset pulse; the time-out tTOUT starts on its falling edge.

A bandgap reference used by the brown-out detector and selectable for the analog comparator or ADC. It is on only while the BOD is enabled by fuse, ACIRS connects it to the comparator, or the ADC is enabled; otherwise it must be given its start-up time before the comparator or ADC result is used.

Counts a separate 128 kHz on-chip oscillator through a prescaler of 2K to 1024K cycles, giving time-outs from 16 ms to 8 s. Modes: interrupt, system reset, interrupt then system reset, and clock monitoring. WDR restarts it. The WDTON fuse forces system reset mode (WDE = 1, WDIE = 0). Clearing WDE or changing the period takes a timed sequence: write WDCE and WDE to 1 together, then within four cycles write the new WDE and WDP with WDCE clear. Reset the watchdog before changing WDP, as a shorter period may expire at once. A watchdog enabled by accident stays on after its reset, so start-up code should clear WDRF and WDE even when the watchdog is unused.

INT0 (PB6), INT1 (PA3) and the pin change inputs PCINT[15:0] trigger even on pins set as outputs, which gives software interrupts. PCINT0 fires on any enabled change of PCINT[7:0] and PCINT1 on PCINT[15:8], masked by PCMSK0 and PCMSK1; pin changes are detected asynchronously and wake the part from any sleep mode. EICRA sets INT0 and INT1 to trigger on a low level, any logical change, a falling edge or a rising edge; a level interrupt repeats while the pin is low. Low level and edge on INT0/INT1 are detected asynchronously. A level used to wake from power-down or power-save must last past the start-up time, or the part wakes with no interrupt.

Two 8-bit ports with read-modify-write: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, value or pull-up without touching the others. Drivers sink and source symmetrically and can drive LED displays directly. Each pin has a selectable pull-up of supply-independent resistance and clamp diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read-only); writing 1 to a PINx bit toggles that PORTx bit. PUD in MCUCR, or PUDx in PORTCR, turns off all pull-ups. Port pins go tri-state during reset with no clock running.

DDxn = 1 makes an output driving PORTxn; DDxn = 0 makes an input, with the pull-up on when PORTxn = 1. Going from tri-state to output high passes through pull-up-on or output-low; where that matters, PUD can disable pull-ups. Moving from output-low to a pulled-up input, or back, should step through tri-state or output-high.

Enabled per port by the BBMx bits in PORTCR. Switching a pin from input to output then inserts a tri-state period of one system clock (250 ns at 4 MHz) before PORTxn appears on it; output to input has none. To avoid glitches, DDRxn should toggle no faster than every two system clocks.

PINxn reads the pin through a latch and flip-flop synchronizer, whatever DDxn holds. An outside change shows after 1/2 to 1 1/2 system clocks. Reading back a value just written by software needs a NOP between the OUT and the IN, a delay of one system clock.

In power-down and power-save the digital input is clamped to ground ahead of the Schmitt trigger so floating or mid-level inputs draw no current, except on pins enabled as external interrupts or held by other alternate functions. A high on an asynchronous interrupt pin set for edge or change, with the interrupt not enabled, sets its flag on waking because of the clamp.

Give unused pins a defined level to avoid input current in active, idle and reset. The internal pull-up does this, though it is off during reset; external pull-ups or pull-downs cover reset too. Tying pins straight to VCC or GND risks heavy current if a pin is set as an output by mistake.

A peripheral takes over a pin through override signals for pull-up, direction, output value, toggle and digital input enable, each with an enable and a value. Enabling an alternate function on one pin leaves the others in the port free as I/O.

As SPI slave, SS, SCK and MOSI are forced to inputs and MISO's direction follows DDA2; as master, MISO is forced to an input and the others follow their DDR bits; a forced input keeps its PORT-bit pull-up. SS low activates the slave. USI three-wire DI does not override the port, so its pin must be set as an input; three-wire DO overrides PORTA2 when DDA2 is 1. OC0A needs DDA2 set. XREF outputs the 2.56 V or 1.1 V reference when XREFEN is set and that reference serves the ADC. ICP1 on PA4 is Timer/Counter1's capture input. The LIN/UART forces TXD/TXLIN to an output and RXD/RXLIN to an input when enabled.

Each OC1Ai/OC1Bi output (U on PB0/PB1, V on PB2/PB3, W on PB4/PB5, X on PB6/PB7) needs its DDB bit set and its bit in TCCR1D. PB7 is RESET unless RSTDISBL is programmed; with DWEN programmed and the lock bits clear it becomes the debugWIRE line, open-drain with pull-up. PB4 and PB5 serve as XTAL1/CLKI and XTAL2 and are then not I/O; with PB4 a clock pin, DDB4, PORTB4 and PINB4 read 0. CLKO on PB5 outputs the divided system clock whenever CKOUT is programmed, whatever PORTB5 and DDB5 hold. USI default pins are DI/SDA on PB0, DO on PB1 and USCK/SCL on PB2.

An 8-bit timer with one compare channel (OC0A on PA2): normal, clear on compare (CTC), fast PWM and phase correct PWM, a frequency generator, a 10-bit prescaler, overflow (TOV0) and compare (OCF0A) interrupts. It can run asynchronously from a 32 kHz crystal or a clock on XTAL1, independent of the I/O clock. CS0[2:0] = 0 stops it.

TCNT0 is compared with OCR0A continuously; a match sets OCF0A at the next timer clock. OCR0A is double-buffered in the PWM modes and written directly in normal and CTC. FOC0A forces a match in non-PWM modes without setting the flag or clearing the timer. A CPU write to TCNT0 blocks any match in the next timer clock. COM0A[1:0] are not buffered and act at once. OC0A drives the pin only with its DDR bit set; COM0A[1:0] = 0 leaves the pin as normal I/O.

Normal (WGM0 = 0): counts up to 0xFF and wraps, setting TOV0 at zero. CTC (WGM0 = 2): clears at OCR0A, unbuffered, so a new OCR0A below TCNT0 misses a match and the counter wraps through 0xFF. Fast PWM (WGM0 = 3): counts 0 to 0xFF, single slope; COM0A = 2 clears OC0A on match and sets it at BOTTOM, 3 inverts; OCR0A at BOTTOM gives a one-clock spike per cycle. Phase correct PWM (WGM0 = 1): counts up then down, 8-bit, TOV0 at BOTTOM; OCR0A at BOTTOM or MAX gives a steady low or high. Toggle on match (COM0A = 1) gives a 50% square wave.

Switching between synchronous and asynchronous clocking can corrupt TCNT0, OCR0A and TCCR0A; disable the timer interrupts, set AS0 and EXCLK, rewrite the registers, wait for TCN0UB, OCR0UB and TCR0UB to clear, clear the flags, then re-enable. With a 32.768 kHz crystal the CPU clock must be over four times the timer clock. Register writes pass through a temporary register and land after two TOSC1 edges; ASSR shows when. Before entering power-save after a write, wait for the update. Re-entering sleep needs one TOSC1 cycle after wake-up. The asynchronous oscillator may take up to one second to settle after power-up or power-down wake-up, and timer registers are lost after power-down. Read TCNT0 after power-save only after writing OCR0A or TCCR0A and waiting for its busy flag. Interrupt flag synchronization takes three CPU cycles plus one timer cycle.

clkT0S is clkI/O by default or the XTAL oscillator / XTAL1 clock when AS0 is set, which lets Timer/Counter0 serve as a real-time counter. Taps: clkT0S, /8, /32, /64, /128, /256, /1024, or stop. PSR0 in GTCCR resets the prescaler.

Timer/Counter1 runs from the system clock or a free-running prescaler tap of /8, /64, /256 or /1024. From enabling to the first count takes 1 to N+1 system clocks; resetting the prescaler affects every timer sharing it.

T1 (PA5) is sampled each system clock; an edge detector makes one count per rising (CS1 = 7) or falling (CS1 = 6) edge, with 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks of delay. Each half period must exceed one system clock: below fclk_I/O/2 in theory, below fclk_I/O/2.5 recommended. Change the clock selection only when T1 has been steady for a clock. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

A 16-bit timer with two compare units, each able to drive four pins (OC1AU/V/W/X and OC1BU/V/W/X), double-buffered compare registers, an input capture unit with noise canceler, CTC, fast PWM, phase correct PWM and phase-and-frequency correct PWM with variable period, a frequency generator, external event counting, and four interrupts (TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B, ICF1). TOP can be 0x00FF, 0x01FF, 0x03FF, OCR1A or ICR1; using ICR1 as TOP frees OCR1A for PWM.

TCNT1, OCR1A/B and ICR1 are reached a byte at a time through one shared high-byte temporary register: write the high byte first, read the low byte first. Reading OCR1A/B skips the temporary register. If an interrupt routine also touches these registers, main code must disable interrupts around the access.

An edge on ICP1 (PA4), or on the analog comparator output when ACIC is set, copies TCNT1 into ICR1 and sets ICF1. Changing the trigger source can cause a capture, so clear ICF1 afterwards. The optional noise canceler (ICNC1) requires four equal samples and adds four system clocks of delay. ICR1 can be written only in modes that use it as TOP. Read ICR1 early in the handler; a new event overwrites it.

Matches set OCF1A/B at the next timer clock. OCR1A/B are double-buffered in all twelve PWM modes and updated at TOP or BOTTOM; not in normal and CTC. A TCNT1 write blocks matches for one timer clock; writing TCNT1 equal to TOP in a variable-TOP PWM mode makes the counter skip to 0xFFFF. A pin carries OC1x only when COM1x is non-zero, its OC1xi bit in TCCR1D is set and its DDR bit is set. Reset clears the OC1A/B state.

Normal (WGM1 = 0): counts up to 0xFFFF and wraps. CTC (WGM1 = 4 or 12): clears at OCR1A or ICR1, unbuffered; WGM1 = 15 is the buffered alternative. Fast PWM (WGM1 = 5, 6, 7, 14, 15): single slope, TOP 8, 9 or 10-bit fixed, ICR1 or OCR1A; TOV1 at TOP. Phase correct PWM (WGM1 = 1, 2, 3, 10, 11): dual slope, compare registers updated at TOP, so changing TOP while running gives asymmetric periods. Phase and frequency correct PWM (WGM1 = 8 or 9): TOP from ICR1 or OCR1A, updated at BOTTOM, always symmetric. Resolution runs from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits. A new TOP must not be below any compare value, and fixed TOPs mask unused compare bits to zero.

Synchronous serial port, master or slave, full duplex on MOSI, MISO, SCK and SS. Data goes MSB or LSB first; seven bit rates from the I/O clock divided by 2 to 128, the divide-by-2 setting through the double-speed (SPI2X) bit. An end-of-transfer flag (SPIF) can interrupt, a write-collision flag guards the data register, and the SPI can wake the part from Idle.

The master drives SS of the chosen slave low by software; a write to SPDR starts eight clocks on SCK and the bytes in the two shift registers swap. SPIF then sets and the clock stops. The master either writes the next byte or raises SS. A slave keeps MISO tri-stated and ignores SCK while its SS is high. Transmit has one buffer, so SPDR cannot be written until the shift ends; receive has two, so a byte must be read before the next one completes or it is lost. In slave mode SCK must stay below fclkio/4.
With the SPI on, MOSI, SCK and SS are inputs in slave mode and MISO an input in master mode; the remaining pins take their direction from the DDR bits.

Slave: SS is always an input; low enables the SPI and MISO (when set as output), high makes every pin an input and resets the slave's shift logic, dropping a part-received byte, which keeps slave and master byte-aligned. Master: an SS set as output is ordinary I/O. An SS set as input must be held high; if it goes low the SPI takes it as another master: MSTR clears, the SPI turns slave (MOSI and SCK become inputs), SPIF sets and the interrupt runs if enabled. Interrupt-driven masters should check MSTR and set it again after such an event.
CPOL and CPHA give four modes. Data is shifted out on one SCK edge and latched on the other. DORD selects MSB-first (0) or LSB-first (1).

A Universal Serial Interface: an 8-bit shift register (USIDR, unbuffered, so read it promptly), a 4-bit counter with overflow interrupt clocked with it, and a two-wire clock unit. It runs three-wire (SPI-like) or two-wire (TWI-like) transfers as master or slave, raises an interrupt on received data, wakes from Idle, and in two-wire mode wakes from every sleep mode including Power-down. The clock comes from the USCK pin, a Timer/Counter0 compare match or software. On an external clock the counter counts both edges. A latch between USIDR's MSB and the output pin moves the output on the edge opposite to input sampling; input is always taken from DI.

Works with SPI modes 0 and 1 on DI, DO and USCK, with no SS logic (software can supply it). In external clock mode 0 (USICS0 = 0) DI is sampled on rising edges and DO changes on falling edges; mode 1 uses the opposite edges. Master and slave load their data and enable their outputs at least half a USCK cycle before the first sampling edge; the master makes each clock by toggling USCK (PORT bit or USITC). After eight clocks (sixteen edges) the counter overflows and USIOIF marks the end; the overflow wakes the CPU from Idle.

operation.topic: USI as SPI master or slave
operation.text: With software strobing of USICLK and USITC, a USI master clocks out a byte in a short loop; writing USICR sixteen times back to back gives the fastest rate, fsck = fck/4. A slave sets three-wire mode with an external positive-edge clock once, then loads USIDR, clears USIOIF and waits for it to set.

Works with the TWI protocol on SDA and SCL but has no output slew-rate limiting and no input noise filter. The master makes the clock in software; both sides shift automatically on the negative edge. The clock-control unit serves the slave alone: it can hold SCL low at the start or end of a transfer to make wait states, so the master checks that SCL really rose. Direction is not set by the hardware; a protocol such as TWI controls it. A transfer: the master pulls SDA low with SCL high (start, which sets USISIF in the slave); the slave holds SCL low after the next falling edge until it is ready; eight bits of address and R/W follow and the counter overflow holds SCL; an addressed slave drives the acknowledge (counter preset to 14) and may hold SCL again; bytes follow in one direction until a stop or a new start.

Active only in two-wire mode. SDA is delayed by 50 to 300 ns to sample SCL safely. It works asynchronously, so it can wake the part from Power-down; the oscillator start-up time set by CKSEL must then be allowed for in the bus's SCL hold time.

In three-wire mode it can speed up a half-duplex software UART. The 4-bit counter can run alone with its overflow interrupt (counting both edges on an external clock), join Timer/Counter0 as a 12-bit counter, serve as an extra edge-triggered external interrupt when preset to 0xF (selected by USICS1), or give a software interrupt from a clock strobe.

A hardware LIN 2.1 controller, compatible with LIN 1.3, or an 8-bit UART. LIN: single master and many slaves on one wire up to 20 kbit/s, slave clocks self-synchronizing to the master, line driver to ISO9141. Hardware handles the header (break, sync, protected identifier) and the response, filters irrelevant frames, detects errors and frame time-outs, supports break-in-data and extended frames, and re-synchronizes automatically. UART: full duplex, asynchronous, high-resolution baud generator, 8 data bits with odd, even or no parity and 1 stop bit, overrun and framing error detection.

A frame is a header from the master task and a response (data and checksum) from one slave task; the master node holds both tasks. Signals sit at fixed places in the data field; diagnostic messages use two reserved identifiers. The master sends headers from a schedule table. LIN 2.1 includes LIN 1.3: a LIN 2.1 master serves 1.3 slaves by not asking them for the enhanced checksum, reconfiguration and diagnostics, baud-rate detection or response-error status. A LIN 2.1 slave cannot run under a LIN 1.3 master. The 2.1 physical layer works in a 1.3 cluster but not the reverse.

Built round the LIN task model: the master and slave tasks meet only at the interrupt that reports a new identifier, raised by the Tx Header function in a master node or the Rx Header function in a slave. Flags mark identifiers 60 to 63 (0x3C to 0x3F). Four interrupts cover LIN: LIDOK (identifier available), LRXOK (response received), LTXOK (response sent) and LERR (errors). Wake-up can use the UART wake-up with at least 5 low bits (0xF0) for LIN 2.1 or 8 (0x80) for LIN 1.3, or a pin-change interrupt. Identifiers 62 and 63 are reserved for user and future formats, reachable through the UART byte mode.

A conventional full-duplex UART with a local loop-back for test. One character of transmit buffering and two of receive (the shift register and one buffer register). Flags are managed automatically as characters are written or read. Receive and transmit are independent, so an unused one frees its pin. The baud generator keeps the error within 2% at any clock frequency and baud rate.

LENA enables the controller; clearing it disables it at once. With LCMD[2] = 0, LCMD[1:0] select Rx Header/LIN Abort, Tx Header, Rx Response or Tx Response. Rx Header/LIN Abort is the resting state: for slave tasks it detects the break, re-synchronizes on the sync field, receives and checks the protected identifier, updates LINDLR in LIN 1.3, starts the frame time-out and watches the bus. Clearing LCMD[1:0] aborts a running function and sets LABORT. Tx Header (master only) sends a 13-bit dominant break, the sync byte 0x55 and LINIDR with its parity bits, then returns to Rx Header with the flags set. Rx and Tx Response are started by the slave task after a header; Rx Response may be given up to the last data bit of the first byte. In LIN 2.1 software sets the response length in LINDLR; in LIN 1.3 the header sets it. LIN13 picks the checksum: enhanced (data and identifier, LIN 2.1) or classic (data only, LIN 1.3); identifiers 60 to 63 always use classic. On an error the transfer stops, flags set and the bus is left recessive. A new break and sync are detected even during a response. Response data passes through a FIFO reached through LINSEL and LINDAT.

With LCMD[2] = 1, LCMD[1:0] choose byte transfer (both services off), Rx byte, Tx byte or full duplex. The LIN FIFO is off: LINDAT is the data register and LINSEL and the LINDLR lengths are unused. Rx: LRXOK reports a character; reading LINDAT clears it, or software clears the flag to skip the character. When both receive stages are full a new character overwrites the second and OVRERR comes with it; FERR marks a framing error. Tx: writing LINDAT clears LTXOK, which sets when the character has gone; there is no transmit buffer and no transmit error detection.

The core reset resets the controller; LSWRES gives a partial software reset. The only clock is clkI/O. LIN13 = 0 (default) selects LIN 2.1, 1 selects LIN 1.3; it only affects the checksum and does nothing in UART mode.

LCONF[1:0] sets the LIN options (standard, no checksum field, no frame time-out, listening) or the UART frame (8 data bits with no, even or odd parity, or listening). The LIN configuration is independent of the protocol chosen. Listening mode joins the internal Tx and Rx lines, disables the TXLIN output and keeps RXLIN enabled, in either mode.

LBUSY in LINSIR shows the controller is busy. In LIN mode, while busy, LINCR (except LCMD, LENA and LSWRES), LINBRR, LINDLR, LINIDR and LINDAT cannot be written. The only commands taken are abort (LCMD[1:0] = 00, acting at the end of the byte), kill (LENA = 0 or LCMD[2] = 0, at once) and LSWRES (at once); any other command is refused, sets LOVERR and leaves the transfer running. In UART mode busy is set only while a byte is sent, locking LINCR (except LCMD, LENA, LSWRES) and LINDAT; receiving does not set it.

While waiting for a header LBT is 32. A break shorter than 10.5 bits or longer than 28 bits (13 nominal) is refused. The sync field (0x55) sets a new LBT, used for the protected identifier and the rest of the frame, then LBT returns to 32. Clock deviation up to ±20% is tolerated and the baud rate is adjusted within ±2%. LINBTR can be used to recalibrate the oscillator in software. No re-synchronization is done in a master node. LDISR disables re-synchronization and lets LBT be written by hand (for a master or for UART baud setting); LBT must be at least 8. A write to LINBTR with LENA set forces LBT to 0x20 and LDISR to 0; with LENA clear it writes LBT and LDISR as given.

During Tx Response LRXDL counts bytes sent; during Rx Response LTXDL counts bytes received, so after an error software knows how many bytes got through. LIN 2.1: a length of 0 sends only the checksum, or takes the first received byte as the checksum; lengths above 8 become 8. LIN 1.3: both fields are set from the identifier's length code before LIDOK, so 0 and more than 8 cannot occur. UART mode forces both lengths to 0 and blocks LINDLR writes; reset also clears them. Error information for a byte is known only after that byte has been fully shifted.

LIDOK sets at the end of a header (not in UART mode); LRXOK at the end of a received response or each received UART character; LTXOK at the end of a sent response or each sent character. LERR is the OR of LINERR: LBERR (bit read back differs from bit sent; transmission stops), LCERR (checksum does not add up to 0xFF), LPERR (identifier parity wrong; software decides what to do), LSERR (sync edges out of tolerance), LFERR (dominant stop bit, also in UART), LTOERR (frame longer than T_Frame_Maximum), LOVERR (command other than abort while busy; in UART, a received byte overwrote the buffer) and LABORT (abort while busy). After any error the controller returns to the resting state. Writing 1 to LERR clears it and all of LINERR.

A break and sync can be detected even when the break overlaps a response byte; the transfer is aborted and the new frame handled. Slaves report LBERR (sending) or LFERR (receiving). A master must itself abort (setting LABORT) and send the new header. The slave detects the break with the old synchronization, so time-out values may be slightly off.

The four LINSIR flags, each with an enable in LINENIR, feed two interrupts: LIN TC (LIDOK, LTXOK, LRXOK) and LIN ERR (LERR). There is no filter on the whole identifier; LIDST in LINSIR only marks identifiers 0x3C to 0x3F, and software sets LIN13 for those frames' classic checksum just after starting the response command.

Response data sits in an 8-byte FIFO reached through LINDAT at index LINDX[2:0] in LINSEL. With LAINC = 0 the index steps after every access and wraps from 7 to 0; with LAINC = 1 the index is written before each access. Byte 0 of the frame is index 0. LINSEL must be set up before use. In UART mode LINDAT is a plain unbuffered data register and LINSEL is unused. A debugger break stops the controller's state machine and frame timer, so traffic may be corrupted.

A 100 µA ±10% source from AVCC, switched onto the ISRC pin (shared with ADC3) by ISRCEN in AMISCR; otherwise the pin keeps its normal function. The current flows through an external resistor and the ADC reads the voltage. A 0.5% resistor is suggested. Make the first reading with AVCC as the ADC reference, then pick a lower internal reference from that result. Use the pin's DIDR bit while the source is on, and switch the source off once the reading is done.

LIN node addressing: each node's resistor gives a voltage that sets its physical address, independent of supply variation. A resistive transducer (thermistor, CdS cell) can be read without a bridge or resistor network. A resistor on the source makes a voltage reference for other devices, or a threshold for the analog comparator on AIN0 or AIN1; a resistor tighter than the source's 2% accuracy is suggested.

A 10-bit successive-approximation ADC: 1.0 LSB INL, ±2 LSB absolute accuracy, 13 to 260 µs conversions, up to 15 kSPS at full resolution. Inputs: 11 single-ended channels on PA[7:0] and PB[7:4] referred to AGND, 8 differential pairs (16 combinations) with 8x or 20x gain, the temperature sensor and the ISRC voltage. Input range 0 to AVCC. References: AVCC (single-ended only), internal 1.1 V or 2.56 V (which can be output on XREF), or an external voltage on AREF with the internal one off, chosen by REFS[1:0] in ADMUX and AREFEN and XREFEN in AMISCR. Free-running, single or auto-triggered conversions; completion interrupt; noise canceler in sleep; unipolar or bipolar differential input; input polarity reversal; optional left-adjusted result.

MUX[4:0] picks the channel and gain; single-ended inputs bypass the gain stage. ADEN turns the ADC on (reference and channel take effect then); with ADEN clear it draws no power, so switch it off before power-saving sleep. The result is right-adjusted in ADCH:ADCL, left-adjusted with ADLAR. Read ADCL then ADCH: reading ADCL blocks updates until ADCH is read, so a conversion finishing in between is lost (its interrupt still fires). With left adjustment and 8 bits enough, ADCH alone will do.

Writing ADSC starts a single conversion; it reads 1 until the conversion ends. A channel change during a conversion waits for it to finish. With ADATE set, a rising edge on the source chosen by ADTS resets the prescaler and starts a conversion; edges during a conversion, or a source still high at the end, start nothing. The source's interrupt flag must be cleared before it can trigger again. Using ADIF as the source gives free running, started by one ADSC write and continuing whether ADIF is cleared or not.

Full resolution needs an ADC clock of 50 to 200 kHz; a faster clock gives a higher rate at lower resolution. The prescaler (ADPS, /2 to /128) suits any CPU clock above 100 kHz; it runs while ADEN is set and is held reset otherwise. A conversion starts on the next rising ADC clock after ADSC and takes 13 ADC clocks; the first after enabling takes 25. Sample-and-hold is at 1.5 clocks from the start (13.5 on the first conversion), or 2 clocks after the trigger edge when auto-triggered, plus 3 CPU clocks for synchronization. At the end the result is written, ADIF sets and in single mode ADSC clears. In free running a new conversion starts at once.

MUX and REFS pass through a temporary register and are locked from the start of a conversion until the last ADC clock before it completes. Write ADMUX no sooner than one ADC clock after ADSC. With auto-trigger, update ADMUX only while ADATE or ADEN is clear, at least one ADC clock after a trigger during a conversion, or after a conversion before its trigger flag is cleared. In free running the conversion after a change still uses the old channel. A single-ended input above VREF reads near 0x3FF. Discard the first result after a reference change.

Conversions can run in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle sleep to cut CPU and I/O noise: with the ADC idle, single conversion selected and its interrupt enabled, entering sleep starts a conversion once the CPU halts; the ADC interrupt wakes the CPU (another interrupt may wake it first, and the ADC interrupt follows when the conversion ends). Other sleep modes do not switch the ADC off; clear ADEN before them.

Each ADC pin carries its pin capacitance and leakage whether selected or not. A selected channel charges a 14 pF sample-and-hold capacitor through 1 to 100 kΩ of series resistance. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less settle in negligible time; higher impedances need longer and suit slowly changing signals. Remove content above fADC/2 with a low-pass filter. For accuracy keep analog tracks short and over the analog ground plane, away from fast digital lines, use the noise canceler, and do not switch digital outputs during a conversion.

An n-bit converter spans GND to VREF in 2^n steps, codes 0 to 2^n-1. Offset: first transition (0x000 to 0x001) against the ideal 0.5 LSB. Gain error: last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) against the ideal 1.5 LSB below full scale, after offset is removed. INL: largest deviation of any transition from ideal after offset and gain. DNL: largest deviation of a code width from 1 LSB. Quantization error: always ±0.5 LSB. Absolute accuracy: the largest unadjusted deviation, combining all of these; ideal ±0.5 LSB.

Single-ended results run 0x000 to 0x3FF. Unipolar differential (the default) requires VPOS above VNEG or reads zero. Bipolar differential (BIN = 1) accepts either sign in two's complement but gives up one bit of range; for full range on a signal of one sign, check the sign (ADC9) in bipolar mode, then convert unipolar with the inputs in the right order.

Selected through MUX[4:0] with the internal 1.1 V reference, read in single conversion mode. The reading rises about 1 LSB per °C. After a one-point calibration at room temperature the accuracy is typically ±10 °C; two calibration points do better. TSOFFSET and TSGAIN calibration bytes are in the signature row.

With the ADC on and XREFEN set, the internal reference is driven out on XREF; a 5 to 10 nF filter capacitor on the pin may be needed. Load current 1 µA to 100 µA, with VCC 2.7 V to 5.5 V for 1.1 V or 4.5 V to 5.5 V for 2.56 V. XREF can be wired to an ADC input.

Compares AIN1 (positive, PA7) with AIN0 (negative, PA6); ACO is 1 when the positive input is higher. Its own interrupt fires on output rise, fall or toggle, and the output can trigger Timer/Counter1 input capture. With ACME set and the ADC off, MUX[4:0] puts any ADC input on the positive side. With ACIRS set, the negative side is the internal 2.56 V reference or a fraction of it (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) chosen by ACIR[1:0]; REFS[1:0] must then be 11.

A one-wire on-chip debug link: program flow control, execution of AVR instructions, programming of the memories, unlimited software breakpoints, real-time and non-intrusive, all functions emulated except RESET. With DWEN programmed and lock bits unprogrammed, the RESET pin becomes an open-drain bidirectional line with pull-up. The system clock stays the CKSEL source. Any pull-up on dW/RESET must be 10 kΩ or more (none is needed); RESET must not be tied to VCC, capacitors on RESET must be removed and other reset sources disconnected.

Breakpoints use the BREAK instruction, so the Flash is rewritten each time one changes, which wears its data retention; parts used for debugging should not be shipped. External reset is not available with debugWIRE on. I/O registers need care when read with the CPU stopped. DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode and raises sleep current, so unprogram it when not debugging. DWDR passes data from the program to the debugger.

The program can rewrite its own Flash through SPM, loading code over any interface. Flash is written a page at a time from a temporary page buffer filled one word at a time; each page is erased first, the buffer filled before or after the erase. To change part of a page, save the rest first. Erase and write must address the same page. The CPU halts during page erase and page write. Page erase: Z selects a page, SPMCSR = 0000 0011b, SPM within four cycles. Buffer load: Z the word, R1:R0 the data, SPMCSR = 0000 0001b. Page write: SPMCSR = 0000 0101b, other Z bits zero. Each buffer word can be written once until the buffer is erased (after a page write, by CTPB or by reset); an EEPROM write during page loading loses the loaded data. The SELFPRGEN fuse enables SPM over the whole Flash; there is no separate boot section.

Z addresses SPM: its low bits pick the word within a page (PCWORD) and its high bits select a page (PCPAGE). LPM addresses bytes, so Z0 is used there. RWWSB always reads 0 on this part. Only the bit combinations for signature read, buffer clear, fuse/lock read, page write, page erase and buffer load take effect. An EEPROM write blocks SPM and software fuse reads; check EEPE first.

operation.topic: Reading fuses, lock bits and signature in software
operation.text: Set RFLB and SPMEN, then LPM within three cycles with Z = 0x0001 reads the lock bits, 0x0000 the fuse low byte, 0x0003 the fuse high byte and 0x0002 the extended fuse byte. Programmed bits read 0. With SIGRD and SPMEN set, LPM reads the signature row byte at Z.

Too low a VCC can corrupt Flash, either because a write needs a minimum voltage or because the CPU misexecutes. Either hold the part in reset while the supply is too low (the BOD, if its level suits, or an external reset circuit; a write in progress at reset still completes if the supply holds) or keep the core in Power-down during low VCC. Flash writes are timed by the calibrated RC oscillator.

Two lock bits set three protection modes and are erased only by Chip Erase. Three fuse bytes hold the clock, start-up, reset, debugWIRE, SPI programming, watchdog, EEPROM-save, BOD and self-programming settings; a programmed fuse reads 0. Fuses are latched on entering programming mode and on power-up in normal mode; changes take effect after leaving programming mode, except EESAVE, which acts once programmed. The three signature bytes identify the device and can be read even when locked. The RC calibration byte (signature address 0x000, high byte) is copied to OSCCAL during reset.

High-voltage parallel programming uses PB0 to PB7 and PA[7:0] as control lines and data bus; pulses are at least 250 ns unless stated. XA1:XA0 choose what an XTAL1 pulse loads (address, data, command or nothing); a WR or OE pulse runs the loaded command. Entering: apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V, hold RESET low and toggle XTAL1 six times or more, set the Prog_enable pins to 0000 and wait 100 ns, apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET with no activity on Prog_enable for 100 ns, then wait 50 µs before a command. The command and address stay loaded between operations, data 0xFF after an erase need not be written, and the address high byte only changes per 256-word or 256-byte window.

Chip Erase (command 1000 0000) erases Flash, EEPROM (unless EESAVE) and lock bits, not fuses; lock bits clear only after the Flash is erased, and an erase must come before reprogramming. Flash: load the Write Flash command, then for each word the address low byte, data low and high bytes and a PAGEL pulse; then the address high byte and a WR pulse to write that page, waiting for RDY/BSY; end with a no-operation command to reset the write signals. EEPROM is loaded the same way a byte at a time and written a page at a time. Reads set OE low with BS1 choosing low or high byte. Fuse low, high and extended bytes are written with command 0100 0000 and BS1/BS2 selecting the byte; lock bits with 0010 0000 (LB mode 3 cannot be undone except by Chip Erase). Fuse and lock bits are read with 0000 0100 and BS1/BS2 choosing the byte; signature, calibration and temperature-sensor bytes with 0000 1000.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over SPI (MOSI PA4, MISO PA2, SCK PA5) with RESET held at GND, after a Programming Enable instruction. A valid clock is needed per CKSEL; with the internal oscillator nothing goes on XTAL1. SCK low and high times must each exceed 2 CPU clocks below 12 MHz and 3 CPU clocks at 12 MHz or more. Data in is clocked on rising SCK, data out on falling SCK. EEPROM writes erase the byte automatically (serial mode only); Chip Erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF.

Power up with RESET and SCK low (or pulse RESET for two CPU clocks after SCK goes low), wait at least 20 ms and send Programming Enable; the second byte (0x53) echoes on the third if in sync, otherwise pulse RESET and retry, always sending all four bytes. Flash: load a page a byte at a time (low byte before high byte per address) and write it with its page address, then poll RDY/BSY or wait tWD_FLASH. EEPROM: write byte by byte (tWD_EEPROM each) or load and write a page; 0xFF data need not be written after an erase. Read back to verify. Raise RESET to run; to power off, raise RESET then remove VCC.

The highest clock rises linearly from 4 MHz at 1.8 V to 8 MHz at 2.7 V and 16 MHz at 4.5 V, staying at 16 MHz up to 5.5 V. The internal oscillator can be calibrated by the user more closely than the factory setting; its frequency depends on voltage and temperature.

The typical curves come from simulation and characterization of similar devices and are not production tested. Current is measured with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on, clocked by a rail-to-rail sine wave. Supply current depends mainly on voltage and frequency, and also on pin loading and switching, code and temperature. Power-down current does not depend on the clock selected; the difference between power-down with and without the watchdog is the watchdog's current. Parts are characterized above their rated frequencies but guaranteed only to their ordering code's speed.

Each peripheral adds its own Idle-mode current when enabled through the power reduction register; at 5 V and 16 MHz this runs from 0.14 mA (USI) to 0.77 mA (LIN/UART), and from 0.02 mA to 0.10 mA at 3 V and 4 MHz.

Rev. C of both devices (Rev. A and B were not sampled). The crystal oscillator (0.4 to 16 MHz) does not latch its gain setting (CSEL[2:0]): the Recover System Clock Source command does not return CSEL[2:0] (no workaround), and the gain changes on the fly whenever CLKSELR changes. Workaround for the second: after any CLKSELR change, write the crystal setting (CSEL[3] = 1 with its CSEL[2:0] and CSUT[1:0]) back into CLKSELR at once.

operation.topic: Errata: Disable Clock Source stays active
operation.text: Rev. C of both devices. In the dynamic clock switch, the Disable Clock Source command keeps running after the targeted source is off, so a different source then selected in CLKSELR would also stop. Workaround: after a Disable Clock Source command, write 0x80 to CLKCSR.
